description: References behind data/traditions/*.json. Every fact in this lane is a paraphrase written for Aleph; no sentences were copied. 'fetched' is the date a page was read in this build session (the text was read through a fetch tool). 'coverage' says how much of the page was read, because some pages were long.

sources.title: Sephardi Hebrew (Wikipedia)
sources.coverage: whole page summarised by the fetch tool
sources.supports: pharyngeal ayin and het among several Sephardi communities; Western Sephardim use a nasal for ayin; alveolar r; tav as t in standard Sephardi and Israeli, th in Greek and some Mizrahi groups; popular speech does not separate patah and kamatz gadol; tsere and holam are plain e and o; shva na read as e; Israeli Hebrew dropped the pharyngeals and shifted resh

sources.title: Ashkenazi Hebrew (Wikipedia)
sources.coverage: whole page summarised by the fetch tool
sources.supports: unaccented tav as s; kamatz gadol as a back rounded vowel (o or aw), u in southern dialects; cholam and tsere regional values; traditional penultimate stress with final stress promoted for Torah reading; ayin, het and aleph silent in most forms; resh varies by dialect; Israeli Hebrew was meant to follow Sephardi values but absorbed some Ashkenazi features; Yemenite keeps kamatz and patah apart but not patah and segol

sources.title: Modern Hebrew phonology (Wikipedia)
sources.coverage: whole page summarised by the fetch tool
sources.supports: older Oriental (Mizrahi) speakers often keep pharyngeal het and, less commonly, ayin; general Israeli ayin merged into the glottal stop; het merged with khaf for most; qof merged into k; resh uvular for nearly all Israeli Jews, alveolar trill often kept by immigrants from Arabic-speaking countries; five-vowel system with no audible length contrast; stress final or penultimate and now meaning-bearing; Standard Israeli based on Sephardi Hebrew

sources.title: Yemenite Hebrew (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: pharyngeal het and ayin; gimel without dagesh as a voiced throat fricative and with dagesh as j; tav raphe as th; dalet raphe as dh; patah and segol sound alike; penultimate stress claim is tagged 'citation needed' on the page, so Aleph does not rely on it

sources.title: Pronunciations of Hebrew (Pealim.com article)
sources.licence: not openly licensed; cited by URL, facts paraphrased
sources.coverage: whole page summarised by the fetch tool; page does not discuss ayin
sources.supports: tav t versus s; kamatz, cholam, tsere values in Ashkenazi versus Sephardi/Israeli; Ashkenazi stress usually penultimate except in public religious readings; het versus khaf and qof versus kaf still distinct in some Mizrahi or Georgian liturgical traditions; traditional pronunciations survive mainly in synagogues and religious schools

sources.title: The Difference Between Sepharadic and Ashkenazic Pronunciation (Chabad.org)
sources.licence: not openly licensed; cited by URL, facts paraphrased
sources.coverage: whole page summarised by the fetch tool; page does not discuss stress
sources.supports: unaccented tav; kamatz versus patach; cholam; tsere and segol; Sephardim distinguish aleph/ayin and het/khaf, Ashkenazim generally do not; many variants inside each grouping; modern Hebrew read with 'Sepharadic' values by many Jews of both backgrounds; the page says all dialects are acceptable

sources.title: Survey of Jewish English and Hebrew usage, popular paper (Benor and Cohen, via BJPA)
sources.licence: not openly licensed; cited by URL, facts paraphrased
sources.coverage: whole PDF summarised by the fetch tool
sources.supports: for the single word 'Festival of Booths', Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative respondents more often chose the Israeli form while Orthodox and Black Hat respondents more often chose the Ashkenazic form; self-reported, snowball sample, not representative of all American Jews, one or two example words only; many people use both forms depending on audience

sources.title: SephardicU guide to transliterating Sephardic Hebrew
sources.licence: not openly licensed; facts paraphrased only, no wording copied
sources.coverage: whole page read through a fetch tool
sources.supports: one Latin letter or digraph per Hebrew letter: aleph silent, bet b or v, gimel g (gh when the soft form is kept), dalet d (dh), he h and always written at the end of a word, vav v (w in some communities), het h, tet t, kaf k, khaf kh, samekh s, ayin an apostrophe (ng among Spanish-Portuguese and Italian Jews), pe p or f, tsadi ss, qof q, resh r, shin sh and sin s, tav t (th when the soft form is kept); patach and kamatz both a, tsere and segol e, hiriq i, holam o, shuruk and kubbutz u, vocal shva e, the ai diphthong, a dagesh shown as a doubled letter (Hanukkah), and articles and prepositions written as separate words (Ha gefen)

sources.title: Benjamin Harshav, Language in Time of Revolution (1993), chapter 27 'Ashkenazi or Sephardi Dialect?'
sources.licence: not openly licensed; the owner supplied the chapter; facts paraphrased only, no wording copied
sources.coverage: the whole chapter and the end of chapter 26 (15 pages)
sources.supports: why the revivers of spoken Hebrew in Palestine chose a Sephardi-style pronunciation around 1900: the prestige of the Jerusalem Sephardi community and of Ben-Yehuda's circle, the 1903 Teachers' Assembly decision, the wish to erase the Yiddish-coloured Ashkenazi subdialects and the sounds of the Diaspora, Biblical final stress; Ashkenazi immigrants found the new accent hard (Agnon, Tsemakh), handwriting stayed Ashkenazi, and old kibbutz speech kept traces such as oMARti for aMARti
